periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Reading Sharma's Story: Chronology and Core Courage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.49): paired discussion on Republic Day, bravery awards, soldier qualities.
Let us discuss (p.59): arrange eight events from Sharma's life in chronological order.

time_bands.activity: Open with the paired warm-up from “Let us read” (p.49): students share thoughts on the Republic Day Parade and name the bravery awards given there. Draw out what qualities they think a soldier must have, then connect that list to the reading ahead.

Teacher reads the prose aloud (pp.49–59) with students following; pause at the key moments — Pakistan’s Operation Gulmarg, D Company’s airlift, the stand at Badgam, and Sharma’s final words — for brief whole-class commentary. This shared reading establishes the narrative arc before any written work.

Students work individually on “Let us discuss” (p.59): arranging the eight events in chronological order (first and last are given). Pairs compare sequences and resolve differences; teacher invites two or three pairs to read their final order aloud and explain any choices that were debated.

periods.teacher_notes: The before-reading discussion about the Republic Day Parade and bravery awards activates schema without requiring any specialist knowledge — accept all reasonable answers warmly. The chronology task is a useful check on whether students followed the narrative during shared reading; if most pairs struggle with the middle events (the Arakan Campaign placement, commissioning date), revisit those sentences in the text together.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis, Inference, and Listening to the PVC

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.59–60): answer inference and assertion questions on Extract 1.
Let us listen (p.66): fill blanks while listening to the talk on the Param Vir Chakra.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.61): choose two ECR questions on Sharma’s legacy and duty to answer in writing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes or directs students to Extract 1 in “Let us think and reflect” (pp.59–60). Students read silently, then the class works through the four questions — the inference MCQ, the fill-in-blank, and the assertion-reason MCQ — orally first, with teacher facilitating discussion of why each distractor is wrong before students write their answers.

Transition to “Let us listen” (p.66). Teacher reads the transcript of the Param Vir Chakra talk aloud at a measured pace while students listen with books closed and answer sheet ready; teacher reads it a second time as students check and complete their five fill-in-blank answers.

Teacher leads a brief whole-class check of the listening answers, asking students to read each completed sentence aloud. Close by connecting the medal’s description — its bronze casting, State Emblem, Vajra and lotus — back to Major Sharma, the first man to receive it.

periods.teacher_notes: For the assertion-reason MCQ on Extract 1, students often confuse Option A and B — accept both in discussion and push students to articulate what distinguishes a ‘correct explanation’ from a ‘true but unrelated reason.’ During the listening, read at natural pace without over-emphasising answers; the second reading is the students’ main chance to confirm, not a dictation.
materials: Printed or copied listening answer strips (optional)

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Speaking on Duty, Writing a Letter of Enquiry

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.66–67): group talk on how students propose to serve the nation.
Let us write (p.67–68): draft a formal letter of enquiry to a memorial incharge.

time_bands.activity: Form groups of four or five. Each group selects a service theme from “Let us speak” (pp.66–67) — saving the environment, health and well-being, helping others, or righteous conduct — and uses the sentence prompts in the textbook to organise a short group presentation. One or two groups share with the class; teacher invites brief responses from listeners.

Teacher introduces the letter of enquiry format from “Let us write” (pp.67–68): walk through the layout on the board — sender’s address, date, receiver’s address, subject line, salutation, body paragraphs, closing. Discuss the four points the letter must cover (visit dates, tour duration, entry fees, student group guidelines) and model one body paragraph together.

Students write their own letters independently using the layout and cues on pp.67–68. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck on the opening or closing conventions. By the end of the band students should have a complete draft; those who finish early check their letter against the format on the page.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking activity works best when the sentence prompts are treated as a scaffold, not a script — encourage groups to add one or two ideas of their own beyond the prompts. For the letter, watch for students who write a personal/informal register; the key teaching point is that a formal letter uses third-person-style requests ('We would be grateful if you could inform us…') and avoids contractions.
materials: Ruled writing paper or exercise books

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Battlefield Idioms, Collective Nouns, and Subject-Verb Agreement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.62): match battlefield expressions to situations and complete sentences A–D.
Let us learn (p.62–63): match collective nouns for armed forces and fill blanks.
Let us learn (p.65–66): fill blanks for subject-verb agreement and correct the passage.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.64): fill blanks with overthrow/overrun/overwhelm and list five 'over-' verbs.

time_bands.activity: Open “Let us learn” (p.62). Students match the four battlefield expressions — fight to the last man, foil the plan, deliver a blow, hold their ground — to their situations in Column 2, then complete sentences A–D using those expressions. Teacher checks answers together and briefly glosses each idiom’s origin in military language.

Move to the collective nouns task (pp.62–63): students match regiment, squadron, fleet, and battalion to their meanings and then fill four blanks. Teacher draws attention to the distinction between army, naval and air-force groupings to help students remember which noun belongs where.

Introduce the subject-verb agreement exercises (pp.65–66). Teacher reads two or three of the ten sentences aloud and elicits the rule at play (intervening phrase, ‘neither…nor’ proximity rule, collective subject). Students complete all ten, then work on the passage correction exercise; teacher leads a whole-class correction at the end.

periods.teacher_notes: The idiom matching often trips students on 'deliver a blow' versus 'hold their ground' — both involve resistance, so spend a moment distinguishing offensive impact from defensive persistence. For subject-verb agreement, the 'neither…nor' and 'each of' constructions are the highest-error items in this age group; use the sentences from the chapter text itself to anchor the rule in familiar language.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Exploring Gallantry Awards and Women in the Armed Forces

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.68–69): research gallantry awards and women’s roles in the Indian Armed Forces.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the passage on Captain Vikram Batra (pp.68–69) aloud as students follow. Contextualise: Batra was the twenty-first and last PVC awardee, Sharma the first — together they frame all twenty-one recipients. Briefly name the three gallantry awards (Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra) students will investigate.

Students work in small groups. Each group divides responsibility — one pair researches gallantry award criteria and examples from the textbook passage and any reference material available in class; another pair notes key roles of women in the Indian Armed Forces mentioned on p.69. Groups compile their findings into a short written list to share.

Groups take turns presenting their findings to the class — one group on gallantry awards, one on women’s roles. Teacher invites the class to add any patriotic songs (in any language including regional languages) they know, making a collective list on the board as a closing tribute to the chapter’s theme of valour and service.

periods.teacher_notes: If library or internet access is unavailable, the textbook passage on pp.68–69 and the prose section are rich enough to support the gallantry awards research; students should not feel stuck without external sources. The patriotic songs list is a light closing activity — accept songs in any language and note regional languages explicitly to include students from all backgrounds.
materials: Reference books or printed resource sheets (if available)
Blackboard for the collective song list

items.item_stem:
Read the events below from the account of Major Somnath Sharma and arrange them in the correct order by numbering them 1 to 5.

(a) D Company was airlifted to Srinagar on 31 October 1947.
(b) Major Somnath Sharma was commissioned into the army in 1942.
(c) Major Sharma correctly identified the first enemy attack as a decoy.
(d) A mortar shell killed Major Sharma instantly.
(e) His men held the position for six more hours before being overrun.

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student sequences events and draws inferences from a narrative prose text using shared and critical reading as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Chronological events of Sharma's life, Battle of Badgam, Extract 1 inference questions on courage under fire.
items.item_stem: When ordered to withdraw during the Battle of Badgam, Major Somnath Sharma refused and declared he would fight to the last man and the last round. What does this decision reveal about his understanding of leadership in a crisis? Support your answer with at least two details from the account of the battle.

expected_elements: Identifies Sharma's belief that retreating would cost Srinagar.
References his actions under fire: filling magazines, laying ground panels.
Notes his responsibility to his 90 men and the wider defence of Kashmir.
Uses formal, text-supported reasoning rather than personal opinion alone.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively to an informational talk and retrieves specific details accurately using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Talk on the Param Vir Chakra: its meaning, design by Savitri Khanolkar, bronze casting, State Emblem, Vajra and lotus.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the talk on the Param Vir Chakra and decide whether each statement below is True or False.

1. The Param Vir Chakra signifies the 'Wheel of the Ultimate Brave.'
2. The medal was designed by Dr. Rajendra Prasad.
3. The Param Vir Chakra is cast in bronze.
4. Four replicas of Indra's Vajra surround the State Emblem at the centre of the medal.
5. The medal was instituted with effect from 15 August 1947.

options.text: Four replicas of Indra's Vajra surround the State Emblem at the centre of the medal.
The medal was designed by Dr. Rajendra Prasad.
The medal was instituted with effect from 15 August 1947.
The Param Vir Chakra is cast in bronze.
The Param Vir Chakra signifies the 'Wheel of the Ultimate Brave.'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the transcript states the PVC signifies the 'Wheel of the Ultimate Brave.'
2. False — the medal was designed by Mrs. Savitri Khanolkar, not Dr. Rajendra Prasad (who instituted it).
3. True — the transcript states the medal is cast in bronze.
4. True — the transcript names four replicas of Indra's Vajra surrounding the State Emblem.
5. True — the transcript states it was instituted with retrospective effect from 15 August 1947.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively to an informational talk and retrieves specific details accurately using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.

items.item_stem: The talk describes both the origin and the visual design of the Param Vir Chakra. In two to three sentences, explain why the designer Mrs. Savitri Khanolkar drew inspiration from Sage Dadhichi, and describe the two visual elements that appear on the face of the medal around the State Emblem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Mrs. Savitri Khanolkar drew on the imagery of Sage Dadhichi, a Vedic rishi, to connect the medal's design to ancient Indian ideals of supreme sacrifice and bravery. Around the State Emblem at the centre of the bronze medal are four replicas of Indra's Vajra, lined with lotus flowers.

items.item_stem: Major Somnath Sharma chose to serve his nation through the armed forces, even at great personal cost. In two to three sentences, describe one specific way you could serve your school or local community — choose the theme of saving the environment, health and well-being, helping others, or righteous conduct — and explain why you chose it.

expected_elements: Names one of the four themes clearly and links it to community service.
Gives a specific, concrete action rather than a vague statement.
Explains a personal reason for the choice.
Speaks in complete sentences with adequate volume and clarity.

items.source_lo: Student organises and presents a structured oral contribution on a civic theme using guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Group presentation on serving the nation: environment, health, helping others, or righteous conduct.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are a soldier who served with D Company at Badgam and survived. A journalist is interviewing you about the battle and asks: 'What kept you and your fellow soldiers fighting when you were so heavily outnumbered?' Respond in a brief role-play conversation of four to five exchanges, using details from the account of the Battle of Badgam and your own sense of duty.

expected_elements: References specific details: outnumbered 500 vs 90, Major Sharma's last words or actions.
Expresses a motivated, reasoned opinion on duty or loyalty, not just bravery.
Maintains the role-play form with clear turns between soldier and journalist.
Uses appropriate register — serious, reflective, not casual or flippant.

items.source_lo: Student composes a formal letter of enquiry following the appropriate layout and register using guided writing as the vehicle.

items.item_stem: Your class is planning a visit to the National War Memorial in New Delhi, which honours soldiers such as Major Somnath Sharma whose names are etched on its Honour Wall. Write a formal letter of enquiry to the Memorial Incharge requesting details on the following four points: (a) available dates for school group visits, (b) duration of a standard guided tour, (c) any entry fees for students, and (d) guidelines your group must follow during the visit. Use the correct letter format with sender's address, date, subject line, and an appropriate closing.

expected_elements: Correct formal letter layout: address, date, subject line, salutation, closing.
All four enquiry points addressed clearly in the body.
Formal register maintained throughout; no contractions or casual phrasing.
Polite request language used: 'We would be grateful if you could inform us…'

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student composes a formal letter of enquiry following the appropriate layout and register using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Formal letter to a memorial incharge: visit dates, tour duration, entry fees, student group guidelines.
items.item_stem: Major Somnath Sharma's citation from the Ministry of Defence praises his personal courage, leadership, and sacrifice. Imagine you are a student who has just returned from a visit to the National War Memorial and seen his name on the Honour Wall. Write a personal blog post of around 120 words describing what you felt, what you learnt about the value of duty and sacrifice, and how this visit will change the way you think about your own responsibilities as a citizen.

expected_elements: Written in first person with a blog-appropriate informal yet reflective tone.
References Major Sharma or the Honour Wall specifically, not generically.
Connects the visit to a personal reflection on duty or civic responsibility.
Approximately 120 words; organised with an opening, reflection, and closing thought.

items.item_stem:
Each sentence below is based on the account of Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam. Choose the correct verb from the brackets to complete each sentence, applying the rules of subject-verb agreement.

1. Neither the enemy's overwhelming numbers nor the devastating mortar fire ________ (was / were) able to break the spirit of D Company.
2. Each of Sharma's 90 soldiers ________ (was / were) determined to hold the position at Badgam.
3. The group of reinforcements ________ (was / were) airlifted to Srinagar in time to save the city.
4. Either the commanding officer or his men ________ (was / were) expected to carry the ammunition magazines forward.
5. The courage and sacrifice of Major Somnath Sharma ________ (continue / continues) to inspire generations of soldiers and civilians.

items.item_stem: The account in this chapter mentions that Major Somnath Sharma was the first of twenty-one recipients of the Param Vir Chakra, and that Captain Vikram Batra was the last. Using the passage on Captain Vikram Batra (pp.68–69) and any other sources available to you, write a short comparison (150–180 words) of the two soldiers: what each did to earn the Param Vir Chakra, and what common values their stories share.

expected_elements: Names the specific actions of each soldier that earned the PVC.
Identifies at least two shared values: courage, duty, self-sacrifice.
Uses evidence from the text rather than general statements.
Organised comparison: not a list but connected paragraphs.

items.item_stem: The 'Let us explore' section notes that the Indian government has taken initiatives to boost the representation of women in the Indian Armed Forces. Prepare a short project (one illustrated page or a set of five to six bullet points with explanations) on the key roles women currently play in the Indian Army, Navy, or Air Force. Your project should name at least two specific roles or branches, explain what those roles involve, and include one example of a woman who has served in or led one of those roles.

expected_elements: Names at least two specific roles or branches women serve in.
Explains what each named role involves in the armed forces context.
Includes one named example of a woman who served or leads in that role.
Presented clearly: labelled bullet points, a short paragraph, or an illustrated page.
